description: Edgehill, Marston Moor, Naseby and the New Model Army — how Parliament beat the King.
content_html:
Taking Sides: Royalists and Parliamentarians

When Charles I raised his standard at Nottingham in August 1642, neither side expected a long war. The King’s supporters — often called Cavaliers by their opponents — and Parliament’s supporters — often called Roundheads by theirs — were largely drawn from the same social world. Both labels were partisan insults at the time, not neutral descriptions. Support divided roughly along religious and economic lines: the north and west tended Royalist; London, the south-east and the navy backed Parliament.

Key Fact

The First Civil War (1642–1646) killed an estimated 85,000 in combat and around 100,000 civilians through disease and dislocation — perhaps 4% of England’s population. The civilian toll is often overlooked.

Edgehill and the Early War 1642–1643

The first major engagement at Edgehill on 23 October 1642 was inconclusive. Prince Rupert’s Royalist cavalry routed the Parliamentarian horse but then rode off the field in pursuit, allowing the Parliamentarian infantry to hold their ground. Neither side could deliver a decisive blow. Charles marched on London but was checked at Turnham Green in November 1642, when a large trained-band force blocked his advance. He retreated to Oxford, which became his wartime capital.

Through 1643 the Royalists gained ground in the north and west. However, Parliament secured a vital alliance: the Solemn League and Covenant (September 1643) brought the Scottish Covenanting army into the war on Parliament’s side in exchange for a promise to establish Presbyterianism in England. This commitment would prove politically explosive later.

The Battle of Marston Moor (2 July 1644) was the largest battle of the Civil War, involving around 45,000 men. The combined Parliamentary and Scottish army crushed the Royalists under Prince Rupert and the Marquess of Newcastle. The north of England fell permanently to Parliament. It was also the battle that established Oliver Cromwell’s military reputation. His disciplined cavalry — which he called “Ironsides” — fought effectively and returned after the charge rather than pursuing, unlike most cavalry of the period.

The New Model Army and the Self-Denying Ordinance

Despite Marston Moor, Parliament failed to win quickly. Part of the problem was military leadership: the Earl of Essex and the Earl of Manchester commanded the main armies but proved reluctant to press their advantages. Cromwell criticised Manchester openly, and in late 1644 Parliament passed the Self-Denying Ordinance. Under this, MPs and lords had to give up their military commands — removing Essex and Manchester.

In April 1645 Parliament established the New Model Army. Its commander was Sir Thomas Fairfax, with Cromwell (who was given an exemption from the Self-Denying Ordinance) as Lieutenant-General of Horse. The New Model was a paid, professional force with a unified command. It was also notably religioniously heterodox — officers and soldiers read their Bibles and argued theology alongside fighting.

Key Fact

The New Model Army, commanded by Sir Thomas Fairfax with Cromwell as cavalry commander, was a unified national force — unlike earlier regional armies. Its discipline and religious motivation gave Parliament the military edge it had lacked.

Naseby and the End of the First Civil War

The Battle of Naseby on 14 June 1645 effectively ended the First Civil War. Fairfax and Cromwell’s New Model Army met Charles and Prince Rupert at Naseby in Northamptonshire. The Royalist cavalry again broke the Parliamentary horse on one wing, but Cromwell’s disciplined cavalry held on the other, routed the Royalists, and then turned on the Royalist infantry. Approximately 5,000 Royalist foot soldiers were captured. Critically, Charles’s private correspondence was also captured, showing he had been negotiating with Irish Catholics and foreign powers — deeply damaging to his reputation.

Charles surrendered to the Scottish army in May 1646, who handed him over to Parliament in January 1647 after he refused to accept Presbyterianism. Parliament now controlled England. But the question of what to do with a defeated king — and who would govern — remained entirely unresolved.

In July 1646 Parliament sent Charles the Propositions of Newcastle, demanding he accept Presbyterianism and surrender control of the army for twenty years. Charles refused. He had no intention of accepting permanent subjugation — he was playing for time, hoping to split Parliament from its Scottish and army allies. His refusal to negotiate in good faith stored up the crisis of 1647–1649. The gap between his public statements of goodwill and private plotting remained a central feature of his kingship throughout.
exam_tip_html: When explaining why Parliament won the First Civil War, examiners reward analysis of turning points rather than a chronological list of battles. Identify the key changes: the Solemn League and Covenant brought Scottish troops; the Self-Denying Ordinance removed ineffective commanders; the New Model Army provided professionalism. Naseby was the decisive battle, but explain why — not just that it happened. Avoid calling both sides “Cavaliers” and “Roundheads” in formal writing; the terms were partisan at the time.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Marston Moor (July 1644) secured the north for Parliament and established Cromwell’s military reputation; Naseby (June 1645) destroyed the main Royalist field army.
  • The Self-Denying Ordinance (April 1645) and New Model Army gave Parliament unified, professional military command under Fairfax and Cromwell.
  • Charles surrendered in May 1646 but refused the Propositions of Newcastle — the question of a settlement remained unresolved, setting up the crisis of 1647–1649.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the New Model Army created in 1645.
practice_questions.marks: Secure: One accurate feature with supporting detail. Example: The New Model Army was a professional, nationally funded force commanded by Sir Thomas Fairfax, unlike the earlier regional armies which lacked unified command and regular pay.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Battle of Naseby in June 1645.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature with supporting detail. Feature 1: Cromwell's cavalry held its discipline, routed the Royalists and turned on their infantry, capturing approximately 5,000 Royalist foot soldiers. Feature 2: Charles's private correspondence was captured at Naseby, revealing negotiations with Irish Catholics and foreign powers, seriously damaging his reputation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Parliament created the New Model Army in 1645.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains multiple causes (Manchester and Essex's failures, Cromwell's criticism of Manchester, need for unified command, Self-Denying Ordinance removing MP commanders) linked together with clear analysis of which was most important. Secure: Two causes with evidence. Developing: One cause or two briefly stated. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: The Self-Denying Ordinance was the most important reason Parliament won the First Civil War. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the Self-Denying Ordinance (cleared ineffective commanders) against other factors: Solemn League and Covenant (Scottish intervention), New Model Army (professional unified force), Naseby (decisive victory), Royalist weaknesses (logistics, correspondence capture). Reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Both sides examined with evidence. Developing: One side primarily. Emerging: Descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Battle of Marston Moor (1644) was significant for Parliament.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Three or more reasons (north secured permanently, Royalist north destroyed, Cromwell's reputation established, Scottish alliance proved valuable, morale shift). Linked argument. Secure: Two reasons with detail. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Vague.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Parliament and its Scottish allies signed the Solemn League and Covenant in 1643.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains Scottish motivation (defend Presbyterianism, obtain English commitment to reform), Parliament's motivation (need for army to stop Royalist advances), and how both sides had different expectations of the agreement. Secure: Two reasons. Developing: One reason. Emerging: Simple answer.

glossary_terms.definition: A term applied to Royalist supporters, originally used as a term of abuse by their opponents; the label carried connotations of Catholic-leaning gentry.
A term applied to Parliamentarian supporters, said to derive from their close-cropped hair as opposed to the flowing locks of Royalist gentry; originally a term of mockery.
The opening battle of the First Civil War, fought in Warwickshire on 23 October 1642, which ended inconclusively.
Parliamentary general who rose to prominence at Marston Moor and later commanded the New Model Army.
An ordinance of April 1645 requiring MPs and peers to resign their military commands, clearing the way for professional, meritocratic leadership of Parliament's armies.
Parliament's professional national army created in 1645, commanded by Sir Thomas Fairfax and Oliver Cromwell, noted for its discipline and religious enthusiasm.
The decisive battle of the First Civil War, fought in Northamptonshire on 14 June 1645, where the New Model Army destroyed the main Royalist field army.

hero_image_caption: Parliament's New Model Army defeated Charles I at Naseby in June 1645.
